title: Buddhism and the Brain
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton takes up neuroscience as a way into the Buddhist teaching of no self, drawing on Iain McGilchrist's The Master and His Emissary and Antonio Damasio's Self Comes to Mind. Shuko describes the left hemisphere as a certainty-seeking tyrant that has undercut years of Zen insight, while the right hemisphere knows connection and can live with uncertainty. Damasio's idea that the self is a process, not a thing, meets the Buddhist teaching of change and contingency, with the slow supermarket line as an everyday example of how clinging to preferences causes suffering. Shuko turns to Dogen's backward step as a way to pause in right-brain awareness, and reports that easing off the left brain's hold has brought some liberation.

sentences.text: Good evening.
So nice to see you all.
I'm very excited to give this talk, not because it's so good, but because I've been thinking about it a long time now.
Last winter when I was shuso, I talked about how my mind worked or doesn't work and my struggle with it, and also about renunciation, giving up self-centeredness.
Since that time, in the spring and summer, I've been reading a lot about how the brain works.
I'm reading a lot of neuroscience, popularized for the lay person.
It has helped me to understand much better some pretty abstruse Buddhist concepts that I've struggled with over the years.
So that's what my talk is about: Buddhism and neuroscience.
I've been struggling also with my voice, as you may have experienced in the past, and it'll calm down in a bit, I think.
So I'll start my talk.
The brain research illuminates core Buddhist concepts.
When the topic is how to deal with life's inevitable sufferings or dissatisfactions, Buddhist teachers tell us to let go of our attachments and preferences.
The Third Patriarch said, *The great way is not difficult.
Just don't pick and choose.

If you cut off all likes and dislikes, everything is clear, like space.* More recently, Buddhist teachers advise us to renounce our preferences and desires for things to be the way we want them to be, or not ask reality to be anything but what it is.
Or simply cooperate with the way things are, instead of always wishing they were different.
The Buddhist first noble truth is that life includes suffering.
We can't escape suffering.
Old age, sickness, death, wars, illness, accidents, crimes, natural catastrophes: we suffer from many things beyond our human and individual control.
And we suffer from a whole lot of annoyances, frustrations, fears, anxieties, angers, emotions that are within our power to control or at least modify.

The emotional, psychological pains that we experience from longing for something that we don't have, from not getting what we want, and from having to endure what we don't like or want, are all sufferings we can mitigate to some extent.
It is these latter types of suffering that I want to talk about, the everyday trials and tribulations of our lives.
In his book, The Feeling Buddha, a book I just found recently on our shelves, by David Brazier, he's a psychotherapist, an American, he said: *the Buddha taught enlightenment.
He did not teach that we will never be depressed or angry or envious or afraid.
He taught us not to be defeated by suffering.
He did not teach us how to avoid suffering.
He taught us to meet affliction and live nobly so that suffering is not unnecessarily multiplied.*
We do have to accept that life includes old age, sickness, and death, but what can we do about the daily dissatisfactions?

You know, the frustration that arises when the telephone solicitor interrupts dinner, or the supermarket line that's long, and yours is always longer than anyone else's, and then there's somebody up at the checker who is very confused and is taking forever to get out of there.

Or the meeting you're in where someone else is rambling on and on and on and the chairperson doesn't do anything to intervene, and you're trying to figure out how you can get out of the next meeting with these people.
Or you said something unskillful in public and there's no opportunity to take it back or to apologize for it.
Those kinds of sufferings, dissatisfactions that set our teeth on edge, make us tense and generally miserable in our daily lives.
We have the teaching of letting go of attachments, having no preferences and picking and choosing.
So why does it seem so difficult to accept things as they are?
Over and over again, I catch myself wanting things to be different from what they are.
I do have moments of contentment from time to time, but much more of my waking life is concerned with wanting things to change or resisting changes that are occurring.
It's so frustrating.
It all comes down to an incorrect assumption I've made about the self whose interests I must protect and promote, I believe.

I've been studying Buddhism for many years, but this nugget of no self, of emptiness, of any abiding nature in all phenomena has repeatedly eluded me until this year when I've been reading about the findings of neuroscience and how our brains work.

With this new information from science, I'm understanding for the first time why it has been so hard for me to retain and act upon Buddhist teachings that I have long since believed are true: the teachings that self is an illusion, and that my assumption that I have a self is actually the root cause of my suffering or dissatisfaction.

Tonight I want to talk first about a classical Buddhist explanation of reality and human experience, and then second about what neuroscientists have learned about our brains that can help us to understand how to work with our minds more effectively, to keep from, as Brazier says, unnecessarily multiplying our suffering.
The nature of mind and suffering according to Buddhism.
Buddhism teaches that it is our fixation on the self that is the primary cause of our suffering or dissatisfaction.
I'm not talking here about selfishness.
I'm talking about self-centeredness, our preoccupation with ourself, which causes us to be unhappy.
This is true not just for the obvious reason that our self-preoccupation cuts us off from other people.
Buddhism argues that self-centeredness is worse than just foolish or unproductive.
Buddhism argues that this view is incorrect because we actually do not have a self.
Now, the explanation of this concept of no self or emptiness is a bit arcane.
The argument goes like this.
Because phenomenon are always changing, they do not have any immutable, enduring self-identity.
Moreover, because phenomenon are made up of parts or aggregates, as the Heart Sutra says, there is no one identity to be found in any phenomenon, including us humans.
The writer and Buddhist B.

Alan Wallace, in The Seven-Point Mind Training, a book that we used in Chris's study group this year, says: *while we perceive our identity as a substantial self, in fact there is no such I as an intrinsic inherently existent self.
I exist only because I conceive of myself.
I mentally designate myself on the basis of things that are actually not myself.
I perform the functions of a person.
I speak, I think, I act, and yet I am not the speech, the thought or the deed.
I am not the body or the mind.
I am designated upon or inferred from the body and mind, and myself depends for its very existence upon this mental designation or inference that I draw.
Like all phenomenon, both subjective and objective, myself does not exist in its own right.*
The Buddhist argument says that because the self cannot be located in one part of my body or mind, the self is nowhere to be found and therefore doesn't exist.
Now, we can follow this abstruse logic, but it's hard to feel convinced by it because even as Wallace acknowledges, things, including ourselves, appear to have independent existence.
But he argues that in this belief in selfhood, we are misconstruing the nature of reality.
Pretty strong statement.
He argues that our belief that we have a self, a separate, immutable, continuous, abiding identity, is our fundamental mistake.
It is this error that leads to our suffering, as I'll try to show.
So what is the nature of reality according to Buddhism?
Quoting Wallace again: *no object exists from its own side exclusively, presenting all of its own characteristics by itself.
Rather, in the act of identifying things, we are co-producers of the objects we perceive.
How does this occur?
As we reach out with the mind in response to events, we identify them as joy, health, ill health, poverty, wealth, and so forth.
We conceptually designate them and we therefore create the world we experience moment by moment.* Unquote.
In effect, then, we make reality up and we make ourselves up.
So all phenomena are the result of co-arising actions or conditions at any given moment.
Because things, including ourselves, are always changing, we are always contingent on other events or beings.
I am who I am, contingent upon my past life experiences, on my parents and other ancestors.
I am who I am right this moment, contingent upon my physical and mental health today and a number of other factors.
I am who I am for you, contingent on your perception and history and current health, et cetera, in response to me right now.
And in a few minutes, all of us will be different from what we were just this minute ago.
It's like that.
So you can see how important it is that we support each other and accept each other, because we're making each other up all the time.
If we want to be happy, we've got to do that together, because that's how it works.
The other side of this coin of things having no permanent identity or self nature is that things are always changing, so they can't have any permanent identity.
Because change is the fundamental constant of life, all our efforts to mold events to suit our desires and to prevent things from changing simply go against reality and lead to suffering.
And lead to suffering and dissatisfaction.
As Wallace says, thinking we can make reality do what we want it to do is our fundamental mistake.
The second noble truth tells us that the cause of suffering is attachment to ourselves and to what we want.
And there is no stronger attachment than to the idea of ourself, that we are and have an abiding self nature that is special, permanent, requires fostering and defending.
Me, me, me.
Of course, our belief that we have a self is why we are self-centered or self-preoccupied.
If we didn't believe we had a self, we wouldn't be so interested in it.
When we can look at our life and experience from the Buddhist perspective and recognize the falsity of our usual thinking and assumptions, we can begin to find some liberation.
So, to review the core Buddhist concepts that explain how things really are.
One, change and contingency.

Because we are always changing, we and all beings, things, exist only moment to moment and are always contingent on other events or beings, co-arising with whatever and whomever we are in relationship.
Change and contingency.
Two, no self nature.
Because we and all things are always changing and contingent on other things and beings, nothing is ever one thing with the same characteristics over time.
Everything is changing.
Thus having preferences for this or that is pretty useless.
When we realize that everything is in flux, we can loosen up on how we respond to experience.
We don't need to grasp or push away, because we realize that everything, including ourselves, is in flux and will soon, soon be different from what it was.
It is our habits of self-centeredness, self-preoccupation and resisting change that make us want to control everything.
But realizing that this is pointless, we can back off a bit, learn to let go of our attachments.
How to do this is the central teaching of Buddhism.
But now recent insights into how our brains work by neuroscience can help us do this.
So, now, how the mind works according to neuroscience.
A book I have found tremendously helpful in loosening up on my reactivity is The Master and His Emissary by Ian McGillchrist, who is a British psychiatrist.
McGillchrist presents recent brain research that corroborates Buddhist ideas about the nature of reality and human experience.
His book is a comprehensive presentation of all manner of scientific brain research, but his emphasis is on the differences between the two hemispheres of our brain.
He says the left hemisphere is the location of verbal language.
It's the hemisphere that is conscious, the one that speaks.
Whereas the right hemisphere, which is primarily unconscious, has some language but can't use it, can't speak it.
It has insight into the relationships and connections of things but no words for expression.
Therefore the right hemisphere appears not to know anything.
And because the left hemisphere can speak, it appears to be in charge of reality.
In fact, the left hemisphere does perform many important functions to ensure our survival.
It has a narrow focused attention, primarily and mainly for the purpose of getting and feeding, that is, surviving.
It is concerned with gaining control over our environment.
It analyzes, categorizes, thinks abstractly.
It has a sequential, linear approach to the truth.
It deals in facts.
It uses denotative language.
It pins things down, makes them clear, precise, fixed.
The left hemisphere seeks control, power, certainty.
That's where it hooks me: the certainty.
The right hemisphere, according to McGillchrist, is largely unconscious, although not totally, on the other hand.
It accesses and inhabits the land of relationships of the individual, ever changing, evolving, interconnected, the betweenness of all things and all beings.
The right hemisphere knows what Buddhism teaches, that we exist only in terms of and through our encounters with other beings and things.
Whereas the left hemisphere is concerned with the survival and prosperity of the individual, the right hemisphere is focused on the connection with other beings.
Empathy and emotional understanding are largely right hemisphere functions.
So it appears that the Buddhist insights into the interdependence of phenomena and the causes of suffering arise through the right hemisphere understanding.
And our persistent self-centeredness and strong attachment to having things the way we prefer them to be appears to arise from the left hemisphere.
McGillchrist says that the left hemisphere can actually suppress meanings that are not currently relevant for survival or efficiency.
The right hemisphere, on the other hand, is always open to all experience.
The right brain seems to accept that life can never be fully grasped, can only be imperfectly known, a stance that the left hemisphere cannot abide.
The left hemisphere must have certainty.
Because the two hemispheres work with experience in two entirely different ways, they apprehend and live with even opposing realities.
In fact, neither hemisphere actually understands the other one, so they can work against each other.
McGillchrist says the right hemisphere needs not to know what the left hemisphere knows, or that would destroy its ability to understand the whole.
At the same time, the left hemisphere cannot know what the right hemisphere knows, because the right hemisphere can't tell it in language.
The two sides of our brains have different goals and capabilities, and yet they have to work together to sustain our lives, so a struggle is inevitable.
Certainly, I have experienced this struggle over many years of my Zen practice.
Time and again, I have understood a core teaching through my right brain, only to have it decimated under the later scrutiny of my logical left brain.
Moreover, because the left hemisphere can't articulate its views and understandings of the world, it argues that what it knows is what is true.
More than that, what it knows is all there is to know.
I, too, have believed my left brain's certainty, and I have come to think of it as a tyranny, actually.
Yeah, like a tyrant.
I find my left brain just bosses me around a lot.
It says, no, no, you can't believe that stuff.

So one of McGillchrist's theses in this book is that in Western civilization, we've become too reliant on our left brains, our left hemispheres, to the detriment of human life and civilization, he feels.
He never says we don't need the left hemisphere.
He just wants us to realize both its strengths and its limitations.
He sums up the differences quite eloquently, quote: *The world, according to the left hemisphere, is a selective, organized, represented, static, revisitable, boundaried, frozen extract of life.

The left hemisphere has taken something life that is infinitely complex, endlessly interrelated, fluent, evolving, uncertain, never to be repeated, embodied and fleeting because alive, and produce something very different that we can use to understand it.
We need the left hemisphere in order to be able to unpack experience, but we need the right hemisphere to fully experience the world.*
In a YouTube video that Elizabeth told me about this afternoon, there's a talk given by McGillchrist, and he quotes Albert Einstein as saying something that's related to what I just quoted here.
Einstein said the intuitive mind is a sacred gift, and he's speaking of the right hemisphere.
The rational mind, the left hemisphere, is a faithful servant.
So the intuitive mind is a sacred gift.
The rational mind is a faithful servant.
Learning how the left and right hemispheres work has explained to me why I have had such a hard time retaining insights I've had from Buddhist teachings.

So strong a hold has my analytic, systematic, proof-oriented left hemisphere mind had on me all my adult life that I have not been persuaded by the very concepts of Buddhism that I have believed were true.
Another book that has been helpful to me in explaining both how the brain perceives and the nature of self is the book Self Comes to Mind by Antonio DiMazio, who's an American neuroscientist.
DiMazio talks about how the brain constructs the mind and how the mind becomes conscious.
His thesis is that the brain evolutionarily and operationally creates a sense of self which is inherent in consciousness.
Of greatest interest to me for understanding Buddhist psychology is what DiMazio describes as our predilection toward feeling we have a self.
He hypothesizes that our sense that we have a self has biological, even cellular, origins.
Our persistent inference that we have a self may thus be deeply embedded in our unconscious.
DiMazio doesn't argue like Buddhist scholars that we don't have a self.
He says, quote, *"There is indeed a self, but it is a process, not a thing.
And the process is present at all times when we are presumed to be conscious."* Any time, he says, the organism encounters an object in the environment, the organism is changed by the encounter.
This is because the brain must adjust the body in a suitable way to respond to the external stimulus.
He's saying, in effect, that phenomena co-arise and co-create each other, just like Buddhism says.
So here is an exciting convergence of Buddhist psychology and neuroscience.
The self is always changing, contingent on our encounters with phenomena, which always change us, so that we and all phenomena are always in flux, in a flow together, co-creating each other.
Due to change, the self is a process, not a thing we can protect or promote.
Still, there is this persistent human predilection toward the sense of a permanent self or identity.
Why is this?
Perhaps our belief arises from the cellular homeostasis process, the built-in dynamic of all living things to return to and maintain balance.
D'Amazio talks about the sense of self being located originally and unconsciously in the brain stem.
He says that as humans evolved and later developed the cerebral cortex, the self came to inhabit the conscious mind as well.
So the sense of self has very long and deep roots and origins.
Another writer who sheds light on this is Rick Hansen, in Buddhist Brain, that Tim talked about at our retreat.
Hansen says, quote, *The self seems unified and continuous* because of how the brain forms conscious experience.
It creates the illusion of integration and continuity.
Many aspects of the self are based on structures and processes spread throughout the brain and nervous system, so that it seems like the self is ubiquitous.
And finally, it is not so much that we have a self as that we do self-thing.
Like D'Amazio, who says it's a process, it's not a thing, Hansen seems to believe that it's a continuous kind of flow.
D'Amazio also writes about the several locations in the brain that contribute to consciousness and the sense of self.
It's a very interesting book.
D'Amazio makes another pertinent observation for this topic.
Remember that he said at any time we encounter an object, the brain must adjust the body to respond.
He notes that the parts of our bodies that interact most with the external world are the ones that are changed: our muscles, bones, limbs, sensory organs.

Our deeper internal organs and structures, our heart, lungs, gut, liver, pancreas, endocrine system and so forth, those parts that are really indispensable for our physical survival, are subject to much less change.
Sensing the relative stability of these core elements in our bodies may contribute to our impression that we have an abiding self.
These scientific observations about our brains and minds have been helpful to me in understanding Buddhist concepts about reality and the mind.
We suffer because we are attached to things being the way we want them to be.
We have preferences because we believe we have an enduring self that must be preserved and promoted.
And we keep forgetting that everything is always changing, including ourselves.
But since nothing is ever one thing, there really is nothing to preserve or promote.
So what can we do with these insights?
Dogen Zenji back in the 13th century says enlightenment cannot be fully understood by discriminative thinking.
Enlightenment cannot be fully understood by the left brain.

He advises us to, quote, *"cease from practice based on intellectual understanding, pursuing words and following after speech, and learn the backwards step that turns your light inwardly to illuminate yourself."*
He uses the word self.
We seem not to be able to get away from it, because we have to say something to point to something.

But the backwards step, I believe, is the step away from our left hemisphere's urgent but inaccurate certainty about reality and into the spaciousness of our right hemisphere's wide awareness, our meditative mind.
Rather than react reflexively and perhaps unskillfully to our experience, we can pause.
We can hang out in our right brain with its priority on connectedness, its patience with uncertainty.
We can experiment with not knowing, at least for a little while.
When we take up the practice of stepping backward into our deeper self, we can explore whatever is there: intuitions, connections, insights, and so forth.
If we still need to meet reality, suffering will still occur.
We may not get what we want, or we may have to endure what we don't want.
But because, as science has shown, the mind can be changed, we can reduce our suffering.
We can learn to meet and accept how things are, just as the Buddha taught.
And when we change how we think, that is, change our minds, we actually change our brains.
The neuronal impulses and patterns actually change, so there's hope.
To help us change the way we think, we can do several things.
We can observe our minds in meditation to see what we are grasping at or resisting.
We can talk to Tim and other practice leaders about our discoveries and concerns and questions.
We can read Buddhist texts, such as Dogen's Genjokoan that we studied on our retreat a couple of weeks ago, a teaching that we explored then that was really wonderful and really on this same topic.
We can read Diane Rosetto's book on changing our behavior through working with the precepts.
This is a book called Waking Up to What You Do that Nancy talked about about a month ago.
Or read this Brazier book, The Feeling Buddha, which proposes that we actually need suffering in order to become enlightened.
He has a really interesting take on the noble truths and the ideas in Buddhism.
There are many books about how the mind works and how we can work with our own minds.
In fact, I've written up a bibliography of what I've been looking at in the last several months, and I'll put this out in the lobby, and you can take a copy if you'd like to.
Concluding, let me read a paragraph that's pertinent here from The Feeling Buddha.
*We are all conditioned in a million ways by our experience.
We do not live naturally.
We live according to our programming.
The effort needed to live the eight-fold path is that of applying ourselves to seeing what is going on in us as it is going on.
We might think that simply to be would not involve us in any character training, but in Buddhism we discovered that only the developed character has the capacity to simply be.
Everybody else is too readily panicked by circumstances to be able to remain calm and in the midst of the whirlwind of life.
The effort that it takes simply to sit still is a good measure of the extent to which we have become alienated from our true nature.*
So he is urging meditation and Buddhist study.
Based on what I've been learning, I've been practicing the backward step lately.
I can report that since I've been less obedient to my left brain's hegemony and have eased up on my preferences, I've begun to feel a greater freedom just to be myself.
I've begun to find some liberation.
I recommend it.
The talk that I quoted from McGillchrist, this writer that's on YouTube, is on the website called TED.
Do you know TED?
T-E-D?
It stands for Technology, Entertainment and Design.
It's a whole series of talks, 20, 30, 40 minute talks by really interesting contemporary people.
You can get it on Google if you haven't seen it.
You just go to TED and you'll bring it up and so forth.
This talk by McGillchrist that Elizabeth sent me this afternoon is illustrated.
You don't see him.
You see somebody doing real fast illustrations and writing all the words that he's saying.
It's really fascinating.
It's sort of a little capsule of what his book said.
I highly recommend that.

She also sent me the other day a really interesting talk by a sociologist whose name is Brené Brown, a Brené Brown woman in Texas who has done a lot of work on compassion for oneself, on being vulnerable and that kind of thing.
There's some really interesting things online.
That's my talk.
If anyone has questions, I would be happy to entertain them in whatever way that I can.
**Participant:** So what is society?
Society seems to be an illusion, but it's very profound.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** For me, the word illusion is kind of tricky.
From what I can understand about this, it doesn't mean that nothing exists, that it's all illusionary.
Things are legitimately there.
It's just that our perception of them makes them what they are for us.
So how we take it in, and then of course we have a lot of opinions and reactions and emotions and so forth to what events outside of us are, that's what creates those things for us.
So whatever we perceive, we have to realize that we need to work on our own reactions and responses to what it is that's out there, because that's the controlling element.
And that's the only thing we do have any control over, actually: how we respond.
So illusion is a word that might lead us to believe that nothing really exists, but everything really does exist.
It's just that what's illusory about it is our opinions about things.

So that's where we need to turn our attention: seeing how we color everything and shape it and distort it, probably, and to work on that part, so we can just let things be what they are, so we don't load anything on them, because that's where we find our suffering occurs.

Because if we either want something that we don't have, or we're trying to resist something that we don't want to have, or we're confused by things and so then we get upset by that, or multiple, millions of different responses, it's in our responses that we need to discipline ourselves and learn to catch them, to perceive them, see what they are, and train our minds to respond differently.
And I think a really extremely encouraging thing to me is that we are capable of changing our minds.

Buddhism has been teaching that forever, but I never got convinced of it until I could see some scientific evidence that, yeah, actually it does change, actually it changes the patterns and the impulses and so forth, and so this is kind of miraculous in a way to me that, yeah, it works, actually works.
I'm sorry I've been a person of so little faith, but that's really the struggle that I've had.
**Participant:** Yeah.

From your study, and you have suggested that you can, does it suggest that we can train ourselves to access the right hemisphere as opposed to allowing the left hemisphere to just be naturally dominant?

**Shuko Edie Norton:** Yeah, I think that's what McGillchrist is saying: give our right hemispheres more of a chance, don't let the left leap in and take over with its various definitions of what things are and aren't, that kind of thing.
Allow uncertainty, have patience with that, allow intuition to arise and trust it.
Insights come in kind of inexplicable ways.
They're not necessarily logically oriented or processed.
Allow for those instead of taking only what is evident, concrete, materialistic, materially evident.
Allow that to happen.
And that takes just sort of stepping back a bit from whatever situation you're in and not demanding that you have an answer right away.
And I think our world is such that we need to be able to prove everything quick and be responsive immediately and that kind of thing.
And we get very, very uptight about that if we can't do it.
And we're not enjoying the real resource in our unconscious that we actually do have, out of which those insights and deeper understandings can occur if we give it the time.
And meditation, of course, is a wonderful opportunity to exercise that wider awareness.
Not necessarily do we sit down to get an insight, but the practice of doing it teaches us how to allow that in our daily life.
And if we have a situation that is really puzzling, which happens a lot, I think, in our life, we can sit down and just calm our minds and maybe an answer will arise in it.
But it seems that that practice helps us to calm our minds so that those things can come to us, come to the surface.

And from what McGillchrist has collected in his study, it seems that the right hemisphere really is thinking about connections and interrelationships and the ineffability of things and how we can't fully understand everything.
So, you know, relax a little, and let it go.
And we'll get further that way than if we're always demanding proof and evidence and that kind of thing.
That's what I think he's talking about.
**Participant:** The only thing I worry about, you know, if you're identifying your...
I personally feel like it's my left brain.
If you're used to it, then you might be categorizing yourself in a way that's also...
Very left brain.
Because you're going to suddenly blame the left hemisphere for stepping in and making things frustrating.
And that will add a whole new psychological problem for you.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** It could.
**Participant:** On the other end of it, being attached, you have wanting the right hemisphere to be more open, you know, active.
So I can see it in a book, too, like the other demonstrate, is given, you know, take it all.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** I think that's right.
And that's a good point.
And he definitely is not trying to say just use your right hemisphere and ignore your left.
Not at all.
He's talking about how they're interrelated in the brain as well.
And I'm not actually saying...
I'm just sort of speaking for myself.

It's been a real revelation to me to realize that the reason that I have mistrusted what I have experienced in my Zen studies and my Buddhist studies is that my left brain, which is very demanding in me, has not allowed me to just accept and, you know, to retain and so forth.
So that's...
It's my experience that I'm really describing.
And I do know that there are people who don't have the same hectoring left brain like me.
But if anybody out there does, I'm happy to share this with you.
But the rest, you know, if you're more balanced than I have been, please enjoy.
**Participant:** Yeah, yeah.
I think it's real organized and plan a strategy to give the right brain...
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Right, right.
And this talk is out of my left brain too, isn't it?
You know, it's the one that talks.
It's truly...
**Participant:** Yeah.
We have to appreciate that too.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Pardon?
**Participant:** We have to appreciate that too.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Yeah, yeah, exactly.
But I'm really very happy to get it off my case a little bit.
This is, let's see, 2009.
And most of the books on this are quite recent.
You know, things have been popping off the shelves at me as I've been...
It's really been fun to have this as a preoccupation for the last six or eight months, because books just sort of say, me, me, me, take me.
And yeah, they are great.
Thank you very much for allowing me to talk about my most recent enthusiasm.

verbatim.text: Good evening. So nice to see you all. I'm very excited to give this talk, not because it's so good, but because I've been thinking about it a long time now. Last winter when I was shuso, I talked about how my mind worked or doesn't work and struggle with it, and also about renunciation, giving up self-centeredness. And since that time in the spring and summer, I've been reading a lot about how the brain works. I'm reading a lot of neuroscience, popularized for the lay person. And it has helped me to understand much better some of some pretty abstruse Buddhist concepts that I've struggled with over the years. So that's what my talk is about, is Buddhism and neuroscience. I've been struggling also with my voice, as you may have experienced in the past, and it'll calm down in a bit, I think. So I'll start my talk. The brain research illuminates core Buddhist concepts.
